senses.gloss: A painting or sculpture that does not show recognizable objects.
examples: A big red *abstract* hung over the fireplace.
The third floor is all *abstracts* from the fifties.
She paints landscapes now, but her early work was mostly *abstracts*.

senses.gloss: Theory or general ideas considered apart from real cases, used in the phrase in the abstract.
examples: Free speech is easy to defend in the *abstract* and hard in a real case.
We discussed the budget in the *abstract* without naming a single number.
In the *abstract* the plan sounds fine, but the details worry me.

senses.gloss: A large machine that speeds atomic particles up to enormous speeds for research.
examples: The lab's *accelerator* runs in a tunnel two miles long.
Physicists use an *accelerator* to smash protons into each other.
Funding for two new *accelerators* was approved last year.

senses.gloss: A short program that gives young companies money and coaching to help them grow fast.
examples: Their startup got into a three-month *accelerator* last spring.
The *accelerator* takes a small share of every company it backs.
The best *accelerators* are harder to get into than law school.

senses.gloss: Approval or welcome from other people.
examples: The new kid slowly won *acceptance* from his classmates.
The idea has gained wide *acceptance* among doctors.
All he wanted was *acceptance* from the people he grew up with.

senses.gloss: A person who helps someone commit a crime or helps them get away with it.
examples: He was charged as an *accessory* to armed robbery.
Driving the getaway car makes you an *accessory*.
Two *accessories* were arrested a week after the shooting.

senses.gloss: A full explanation of what happened or of how something was used.
examples: The families want a full *accounting* of the mistakes made that night.
Voters are owed an *accounting* of where the money went.
No *accounting* of the missing hours was ever given.

senses.gloss: Knowledge or experience of something, gained by having dealt with it.
examples: She has a passing *acquaintance* with Spanish.
His *acquaintance* with the law comes from years as a court reporter.
I have only a slight *acquaintance* with that part of the city.

senses.gloss: The gaining of a skill, a habit, or knowledge.
examples: The book is about language *acquisition* in small children.
Vocabulary *acquisition* speeds up once you start reading novels.
Skill *acquisition* takes steady practice, not talent.

senses.gloss: Clever, complicated maneuvering with words, numbers, or ideas.
examples: It took real verbal *acrobatics* to avoid answering the question.
The budget balances only after some accounting *acrobatics*.
No amount of legal *acrobatics* will make that contract valid.

senses.gloss: A feature or behavior that has developed to help a living thing survive where it lives.
examples: Thick fur is an *adaptation* to the cold.
The cactus has several *adaptations* for storing water.
Long legs are an *adaptation* for running in open country.

senses.gloss: The process of changing in order to fit new conditions.
examples: *Adaptation* to life in a new country takes a year or two.
Coastal cities are spending billions on climate *adaptation*.
His *adaptation* to the night shift was slow and painful.

senses.gloss: The work of managing an organization, or the people who do that work.
examples: She works in hospital *administration*.
The school *administration* canceled the field trip.
Too much of his day goes to *administration* and not enough to teaching.

senses.gloss: The giving of a drug, a treatment, or a test.
examples: The *administration* of the vaccine takes about a minute.
Nurses record the time of each *administration*.
*Administration* of the exam was delayed by the storm.

senses.gloss: The act of starting to use or accept something new.
examples: The *adoption* of electric buses saved the city money.
Wide *adoption* of the app took about two years.
The board voted for *adoption* of the new safety rules.

senses.gloss: A later effect or reaction that follows a shocking event.
examples: The layoffs sent *aftershocks* through the whole town.
We are still feeling the *aftershocks* of that decision.
The scandal's political *aftershocks* lasted for years.

senses.gloss: A feeling, usually an unpleasant one, that stays with you after an experience.
examples: The whole argument left a bitter *aftertaste*.
Winning that way leaves a bad *aftertaste*.
There was a sour *aftertaste* to the entire deal.

senses.gloss: Angry or violent behavior or feelings toward other people.
examples: The dog showed *aggression* toward strangers.
He gets into fights and can't control his *aggression*.
Teachers watch for signs of *aggression* on the playground.

senses.gloss: The state of holding the same opinion as someone else.
examples: The committee is in *agreement* about the deadline.
There was broad *agreement* that the plan needed work.
We are in complete *agreement* on that point.

senses.gloss: In grammar, the matching of words with each other in number, person, or gender.
examples: Subject-verb *agreement* trips up a lot of writers.
In Spanish there is *agreement* between the noun and the adjective.
The sentence has an *agreement* error in the second clause.

senses.gloss: A burden or problem that someone is stuck with and cannot get rid of.
examples: The empty mall became an *albatross* for the county.
That loan is an *albatross* around his neck.
The old contract is an *albatross* the team can't shake.

senses.gloss: An amount of something that is officially permitted.
examples: Your baggage *allowance* is one checked bag.
The daily salt *allowance* is smaller than most people think.
Both airlines cut their carry-on *allowances*.

senses.gloss: Extra understanding given because of someone's circumstances, used mainly in the phrase make allowances.
examples: You have to make *allowances* for how tired he was.
The teacher made *allowances* for the students who had been sick.
Even making *allowances* for the weather, the crew was slow.

senses.gloss: A well-known person chosen to represent and promote a product, a sport, or a cause.
examples: She signed on as a brand *ambassador* for the shoe company.
He has been a great *ambassador* for the sport.
The charity named three new *ambassadors* this year.

senses.gloss: Facts or information used to attack someone in an argument.
examples: The leaked emails gave his critics plenty of *ammunition*.
Don't hand them *ammunition* by missing the deadline.
Every small mistake became *ammunition* for the other side.
